strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and timely gap: existing reward benchmarks (RewardBench, RM-Bench) evaluate pairwise preference ranking, while reasoning-model RL training increasingly relies on reference-based verification. The proposed VerifyBench/VerifyBench-Hard fill a real evaluation need.

Benchmark construction is reasonably careful and transparent: queries curated from 41 diverse sources, completions generated by 22 open and proprietary LLMs, dual human annotation with a third-annotator adjudication process, and controlled downsampling for balanced answer-type and correctness distributions.

The evaluation is comprehensive: rule-based baselines (math-verify), a wide range of LLM-as-a-judge models across sizes, reference-free reward models, an ablation on reference-answer presence (Table 3), a fine-grained error taxonomy with actionable error analysis (Table 5), and a downstream correlation study using rejection-sampling fine-tuning (RFT) with three verifiers of differing benchmark accuracy.

VerifyBench-Hard, built via systematic model-disagreement filtering, is a sensible design for differentiating models, and the reported results (72.4% best accuracy vs ~96% on the standard set) substantiate the claim that hard cases remain open.

Limitations are honestly discussed (limited domains, no reward-hacking evaluation, binary labels, excluded proof problems), and supporting material (prompts, data sources, licenses, hyperparameters) is provided, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Modest novelty relative to prior work: verifier/judge evaluation benchmarks and error taxonomies exist (e.g., ProcessBench, VerifierBench-style efforts), and the delta—shifting from pairwise preference to single-reference verification—is more an incremental reframing than a fundamentally new methodology.

Benchmark size is small: 2,000 tuples for VerifyBench and 1,000 for VerifyBench-Hard, with only 1,000 and 945 unique questions respectively. Sub-category analyses (e.g., 8 numeric subtypes) operate on very few samples, making fine-grained conclusions statistically fragile.

Potential label-quality circularity: initial correctness labels come from Llama-3.3-70B pre-annotation, and VerifyBench-Hard is selected precisely in the regime where strong LLM judges disagree—these are exactly the ambiguous cases where human labels themselves are least reliable. No inter-annotator agreement statistics (e.g., Cohen's kappa) are reported, so label quality is hard to verify.

Dataset-design artifacts: VerifyBench enforces exactly one correct and one incorrect completion per question, so the marginal probability is 50% and a solver can exploit the balance; the Hard set's natural skew (709 incorrect vs 291 correct) changes the task between the two benchmarks, complicating direct comparison. Completeness of human answers on the RFT experiments also only shows small absolute differences among three verifiers on math-only tasks, which is a narrow validation of 'correlation with real-world RL'.

Contamination risk is not analyzed: many questions come from widely used benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH, GPQA, MMLU-Pro, BBH) that evaluated verifier models have likely seen during pretraining, which could inflate measured verification accuracy.

Some presentation issues: typos (e.g., 'Reasonoing', 'Refence'), example figures where reference/completion content appears swapped (Figure 7), and a binary scoring scheme that ignores partially correct reasoning, as the authors themselves acknowledge.

The related-work positioning of process-level benchmarks (ProcessBench, PRM800K) is brief in the main text and does not empirically compare against them, leaving the claimed uniqueness of the benchmark less rigorously established.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and timely gap: existing reward-model benchmarks (RewardBench, RM-Bench) evaluate pairwise preference ranking, whereas modern reasoning-RL pipelines rely on reference-based verification. Formalizing and benchmarking this setting (Eq. 2 vs. Eq. 3-4) is a useful conceptual contribution.

The construction pipeline is reasonably thorough: 41 data sources across three reasoning domains, ~1.45M completions from 22 models, balanced answer-type/domain/correctness design, and double human annotation with a third-annotator adjudication protocol.

The evaluation covers a broad set of systems (rule-based math-verify, 16 LLM-as-judge models, and 6 reference-free reward models), and the ablation removing reference answers (5-18% degradation, Table 3) directly supports the paper's motivating claim.
The correlation analysis (Section 5.2) attempting to link benchmark accuracy to downstream RFT outcomes is a good instinct, as benchmark-only papers often lack evidence of practical utility.
Limitations are candidly discussed (domain coverage, annotation bias, reward hacking, binary scoring, exclusion of proof problems).
weaknesses: Limited novelty beyond the framing. The core evaluation is standard LLM-as-a-judge accuracy against human labels; there is no new methodology, and the 'hard' variant is a disagreement-filtered subsample, which is a common technique (e.g., RewardBench-style filtering). For a benchmark paper, the dataset and analysis need to be exceptional, and this falls short of that bar.

Potential circularity/contamination in construction and evaluation. Completions are generated by many of the same model families (Qwen, Llama, DeepSeek, etc.) that are then evaluated as judges; e.g., Qwen3 models both generate completions and top the leaderboard (Qwen3-32B, 95.8% / 71.8%). Self-verification bias and possible contamination of judge models with the source datasets are not analyzed.

VerifyBench-Hard is constructed by disagreement among five specific judge models, several of which appear in the main evaluation; models in that selection committee have a structural advantage/disadvantage, and 'hardness' is defined relative to a fixed, non-released set of judges rather than an intrinsic property.

The correlation analysis is weak support for the headline claim of 'alignment with real-world RL': it uses only three verifiers, applies rejection-sampling SFT rather than actual RL, differences in Figure 3 are small (often <1-2 points), and no error bars or multiple seeds are reported. One favorable ordering among three verifiers is thin evidence.

The benchmark is small and partially skewed: VerifyBench has only 1,000 unique questions / 2,000 tuples (and each question's correct/incorrect pair comes from pre-annotated four completions, which conditions on Llama-3.3-70B judgment quality), while VerifyBench-Hard is unbalanced (291 correct vs. 709 wrong), complicating interpretation of raw accuracy.

Missing comparisons and analyses that would strengthen significance: no evaluation of process reward models (despite citing ProcessBench/ThinkPRM), no analysis of whether judge performance transfers to the open-ended/general domain, no statistical significance testing for category-level gaps, and no discussion of judge position/format sensitivity.

Reproducibility and clarity issues: the release of data/prompts is not clearly stated; there are typographical and caption errors (e.g., 'Refence Answer', 'Reasoing', Figure 6 caption says 'with a reference answer' for the no-reference prompt), and Figure 7's example shows reference/completion content that appears inconsistent with the stated roles.

Several conclusions are over-claimed relative to evidence, e.g., 'establish a standardized framework for improving verification accuracy, ultimately enhancing reasoning capabilities' when the downstream experiment is a limited SFT setup with three verifiers.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and timely gap: existing reward benchmarks (RewardBench, RM-Bench) evaluate pairwise preference ranking, while reasoning-model RL pipelines (DeepSeek-R1, Seed1.5-Thinking) rely on reference-based correctness verification. The problem formulation (Eq. 3-4) cleanly distinguishes this setting from prior work.

Careful, transparent benchmark construction: questions aggregated from 41 documented sources with license information, completions generated by 22 diverse open/proprietary models, pre-annotation plus at least two independent human annotators with third-annotator arbitration for disagreements, and controlled downsampling for balanced answer-type/domain/correctness distributions.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning rule-based verifiers (math-verify), 17 LLM-as-a-judge models, and 6 reference-free reward models, with a useful ablation showing 5-18% degradation when reference answers are removed (Table 3) — strong evidence for the benchmark's core thesis.

The RFT correlation experiment (Section 5.2) goes beyond static benchmarking by demonstrating alignment between VerifyBench accuracy and downstream downstream training outcomes across GSM8K/MATH500/SVAMP, which addresses the standard criticism of benchmark-only papers.

Fine-grained error taxonomy (Table 5) yields actionable insights (e.g., order-invariance of multi-value answers, mathematical equivalence vs. surface form), and the Limitations section is honest and specific (domain coverage, annotation bias, reward hacking, binary scoring).
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the construction pipeline (LLM generation + LLM pre-labeling + human annotation + filtering/downsampling) is standard for benchmark papers. The main contribution is the benchmark itself, so its long-term value depends heavily on adoption, which is not yet demonstrated.

Potential circularity/bias in labeling: Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct performs pre-annotation and is also an evaluated system, and the LLM-as-a-judge ground-truthing process may favor verifiers stylistically similar to the annotator model. No inter-annotator agreement statistics (e.g., Cohen's kappa) are reported, so label quality is asserted rather than quantified.

Modest benchmark scale: 2,000 tuples (VerifyBench) and 1,000 tuples (VerifyBench-Hard) is small relative to modern benchmarks; small per-subcategory cells (e.g., 88 expression samples in VerifyBench-Hard) make fine-grained analyses statistically fragile, and no confidence intervals or significance tests are provided.

VerifyBench-Hard is imbalanced by construction (291 correct vs. 709 incorrect), which complicates accuracy-based comparison and rewards degenerate 'always wrong' predictors (majority-class accuracy of ~71% is close to the best reported score of 72.4%); balanced accuracy or per-class metrics would strengthen the conclusions. The 2-of-5 disagreement selection rule is also somewhat ad hoc.

Correlation analysis (Section 5.2) is narrow: only three verifier models, only mathematical tasks, only rejection-sampling SFT rather than the RL setting the benchmark nominally targets; the claim that VerifyBench 'serves as a reliable tool to guide development' rests on limited evidence. Reward hacking — a central motivation cited in the introduction — is acknowledged as unaddressed.

The rule-based baseline (math-verify) is nearly inapplicable to multi-choice and string categories (8-19% accuracy), making cross-category comparisons in Table 2 partly uninformative; no process reward models (e.g., ThinkPRM-style) are evaluated despite the related-work discussion.

Possible data contamination concerns: questions are drawn from widely used public benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH, BBH, etc.) that evaluation models have likely seen during training, which could confound verifier accuracy measurements; no decontamination or contamination analysis is reported.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and timely gap: existing reward benchmarks (RewardBench, RM-Bench, RMB) evaluate pairwise preference, while modern reasoning-model RL (RLVR/GRPO) relies on reference-based verification; VerifyBench is a focused, well-motivated instrument for this use case.

Careful, transparent data construction: 41 diverse sources across general/logic/math reasoning, 22 generators, automated pre-annotation, and two-annotator-plus-meta-annotator human labeling with documented training, instructions, and UI (Appendix F).

VerifyBench-Hard uses a principled disagreement-based selection strategy to target cases where strong models diverge, yielding a substantially harder test (best accuracy ~88% vs ~96%, with many systems below 55%).

Broad evaluation coverage: rule-based (math-verify), ~20 LLM-as-a-judge models across families/sizes, and dedicated model-based verifiers (xVerify, CompassVerifier, Tencent-RLVR), plus a reference-ablation (Table 3) that cleanly quantifies the value of reference answers (5-18% degradation).

Beyond static benchmark scores, the paper validates practical utility through real GRPO training and RFT experiments, showing verifier accuracy on VerifyBench correlates with downstream RL gains - a validation many benchmark papers lack.

Good reproducibility support: full prompt templates, dataset licenses, generation hyperparameters, RL/RFT training details, and example data; clearly written limitations section (domain coverage, annotation bias, reward hacking, binary scoring).
weaknesses: VerifyBench is near-saturated (top systems 94-96%), limiting its discriminative power, while the effective size is small (1,000 questions / 2,000 tuples); the Hard variant is only 1,000 tuples, making fine-grained subgroup comparisons (e.g., only 88 expression cases in VB-H) statistically noisy.

VerifyBench-Hard has a strongly skewed label distribution (709 incorrect vs 291 correct) and imbalanced answer-type coverage; plain accuracy is confounded by class priors and balanced-accuracy or per-class metrics are not reported.

Selecting Hard samples precisely where models disagree risks label ambiguity and elevated annotation noise in exactly the hardest cases; no inter-annotator agreement statistics (e.g., Cohen's kappa) are reported to quantify label reliability.

Thresholding/discretization for model-based verifiers (the E(.) operator in Eq. 4) is underspecified, and evaluation protocol details for model-based verifiers could affect comparability across systems.

Benchmark relies exclusively on binary correctness and excludes proof-based/open-ended questions, limiting coverage of real RLVR settings; hard-set completions exclude closed-source models, potentially narrowing difficulty diversity.

Contamination risk: questions are drawn from widely used public benchmark test sets (MATH, GPQA, MMLU-Pro, etc.) without decontamination analysis, and the reference answers come directly from these sources.

The RL correlation analysis uses a single base model, a single dataset (DeepMath-103K), math-only downstream tasks, and apparently single-run training without seed variance, so the claimed correlation between benchmark accuracy and RL utility rests on a narrow empirical base.

Some sloppiness in presentation (typos such as 'Reasonoing', 'Refence Answer', minor grammatical errors, inconsistent statistics references) and the easy/hard benchmark naming may confuse against concurrent VerifierBench work, which is only briefly differentiated.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and timely gap: existing reward-model benchmarks (RewardBench, RM-Bench, RMB) focus on pairwise preference ranking, while modern reasoning-model training relies on reference-based verification, which has not been systematically benchmarked.

The data construction pipeline is reasonably careful: 41 data sources across three reasoning domains, 22 completion-generating models, at least two human annotators per instance with meta-annotator adjudication, and a disagreement-based difficulty filtering strategy for the Hard variant.

The evaluation covers a broad range of systems (rule-based verifiers, 20+ LLM-as-a-judge models, dedicated verifiers like xVerify and CompassVerifier, and reference-free reward models), providing a useful reference snapshot.

The correlation analysis (Section 5.2, Appendix H), showing that verifier accuracy on VerifyBench correlates with downstream RL (GRPO) and RFT training outcomes, adds practical credibility beyond static leaderboard numbers.
The ablation in Table 3 (5–18% accuracy drop without reference answers) is a clean, informative experiment that supports the paper's core motivation.
Reproducibility artifacts are comparatively thorough: prompts, annotation interfaces, annotator qualifications, dataset licenses, and training configurations are documented in the appendix.
weaknesses: Limited novelty and significant overlap with concurrent work: the paper itself acknowledges (Appendix B.2) that VerifierBench (Liu et al., 2025a) employs a similar construction. The main differentiators (more data sources, disagreement-based Hard split) are incremental, weakening the case for a dedicated benchmark paper.

VerifyBench is nearly saturated: top systems reach 92–96% accuracy, so the standard split offers limited discriminative power for future model development, undermining its stated purpose as a 'standardized framework for improving verification accuracy'.

VerifyBench-Hard has a severe label imbalance (709 incorrect vs. 291 correct completions), which makes raw accuracy misleading — a trivial majority-class baseline achieves ~71%, above many evaluated systems. No balanced accuracy, AUROC, or F1 is reported, and this imbalance is a design artifact of 'natural sampling' rather than a deliberate, well-justified choice.

Potential circularity/selection bias in VerifyBench-Hard: the five LLMs used for difficulty filtering (Llama-3.3-70B, Llama-4-Scout, Qwen2.5-72B, Qwen3-30B/32B) are also among the evaluated systems, so the Hard benchmark is constructed using disagreement from models that are later scored on it, which complicates interpretation of their results.

Small benchmark size: 1,000 questions / 2,000 completions (and 1,000 tuples for the Hard variant) limits statistical power for fine-grained subcategory analyses in Table 5, where per-subtype counts are very small.

The annotation team is small (4 primary annotators, all students) and no inter-annotator agreement statistics (e.g., Cohen's kappa) are reported, making the claimed label quality hard to verify independently.

The rule-based baseline result is suspicious: math-verify scores 19.4% on multi-choice and 8.6% on string answers, which likely reflects harness/parsing issues rather than the method's capability; the fairness of this baseline is questionable and unexamined.

Domain coverage is narrow (general/logic/math reasoning, with math dominating; proofs explicitly excluded), and the binary correct/incorrect labeling cannot capture partially correct or process-level errors — both acknowledged in Limitations but not resolved.

The RL correlation experiment uses a single base model (Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct), a single training set (DeepMath-103K), and only math evaluation tasks; the 'correlation' is based on four verifier choices with widely different sizes/capabilities, so the evidence that VerifyBench predicts RL utility is suggestive rather than convincing.

Writing quality issues (e.g., 'Refence Answer' in Figure 1, grammatical errors in Section 1) and the large claim-to-evidence gap in the abstract ('provide insights for advancing reference-based reward systems') slightly undercut polish.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and timely gap: existing reward benchmarks (RewardBench, RM-Bench, RMB) are preference-based, while modern reasoning RL (RLVR) relies on reference-based verification, which has lacked systematic evaluation.

Careful and transparent benchmark construction: questions drawn from 41 sources across general/logic/math reasoning, completions from 22 diverse open- and closed-source generators, and every instance double-annotated by humans with meta-annotator arbitration. The annotation protocol, annotator backgrounds, UI, and prompts are documented in detail (Appendices E, F), which is above-average rigor for benchmark papers.

Comprehensive evaluation spanning rule-based verifiers (math-verify), LLM-as-a-judge across ~20 models, and specialized model-based verifiers (xVerify, CompassVerifier), with balanced answer-type and domain stratification.

Useful analyses beyond a leaderboard: an ablation showing 5-18% degradation without reference answers, a fine-grained error taxonomy identifying systematically error-prone subtypes (multi-value numbers, unsimplified expressions, semantic strings), and a downstream correlation study showing verifier accuracy on VerifyBench predicts RL/RFT training outcomes - the latter is a strong practical validation that most benchmark papers omit.
VerifyBench-Hard, built from inter-model disagreement, meaningfully separates strong verifiers (~88%) from the pack and demonstrates clear headroom (72.4% best vs ~95% on VerifyBench).
weaknesses: Contamination risk is not addressed: questions and reference answers are drawn from public benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH, AIME, GPQA, etc.), and the evaluated LLM-as-judge models have very likely seen these questions and answers during pretraining. No decontamination check or discussion is provided, which may inflate VerifyBench scores.

Modest benchmark size: 1,000 questions / 2,000 completions (VB) and 1,000 tuples (VB-H) are small for a lasting benchmark; per-subtype analyses in Table 5 rest on very few samples (some subcategory deltas are computed on tens of instances), making fine-grained conclusions statistically fragile.

Circularity in VerifyBench-Hard: difficulty is defined by disagreement among five models, several of which (Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen family) are also evaluated in the results table; pre-annotation was performed by Llama-3.3-70B with humans only checking/correcting, so residual pre-annotation bias may persist in both sets.

VerifyBench-Hard is naturally imbalanced (709 wrong vs 291 correct), so raw accuracy conflates calibration with correctness; a majority-class baseline (~71%) makes several reported 'Hard' scores less impressive than presented, and no balanced-metric (F1/balanced accuracy) is reported.

Some inconsistent/unclear reporting: Table 1 lists 945 unique questions for 1,000 completions in VB-H; the disagreement-filtering rule (two models vs three) is somewhat arbitrary; details of thresholding E(·) for model-based verifiers are sparse.
Novelty is partly eroded by the acknowledged concurrent work VerifierBench (Liu et al., 2025a); the main differentiators (41 vs 14 sources, the Hard split) are incremental rather than conceptual.

Correlation analysis is thin: a single base model (Qwen2.5-3B), a single RL algorithm, and only four verifiers, with qualitative reading of curves rather than a quantitative correlation coefficient; the claim that VerifyBench 'guides RL training' would benefit from broader evidence.
Reproducibility specifics (data release, evaluation code, exact decoding settings for judged models) are not clearly stated in the main text.
